passage: Teacher's note, Tuesday. At outdoor time, Parul wanted the slide straight away and tried to climb up the front. I reminded her, 'The line starts here. You're after Sunaina.' She stamped her foot and hopped from side to side, counting the children out loud. I told her, 'You're waiting so well. One more turn.' When Sunaina went down, Parul shrieked with joy and zoomed after her. Tomorrow I will put turn cards at the slide so the order is easy to see.

qa.q: Who was Parul waiting after?
qa.a: Sunaina.

qa.q: What does Parul hopping from side to side suggest?
qa.a: She felt impatient and restless, finding it hard to wait for her turn.

qa.q: What is the teacher planning, and why might it help?
qa.a: Putting turn cards at the slide so the order is easy to see, which makes waiting feel clear and fair.

qa.q: How might Sunaina feel when Parul tried to climb up the front?
qa.a: Sunaina may have felt worried or cross that her turn would be taken, and relieved when the teacher kept the order.

grounding: A young child finds waiting for the slide hard and holds on with adult praise and a clear, fair order.

passage: At the village ration shop in Punjab, the line stretched past the neem tree. Rukmini held Nani's hand and hopped. 'Why can't we go first?' she whined. 'Because Jeeto aunty came first,' Nani said. Rukmini pulled at Nani's dupatta and groaned loudly. Amandeep, the shopkeeper, called out, 'Who's the best waiter in this line?' Rukmini stood very still. When their turn came, he gave her a small paper cone of roasted chana. 'For waiting,' he said. Rukmini grinned all the way home.

qa.q: Where did the line stretch to?
qa.a: Past the neem tree.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling when she groaned and pulled Nani's dupatta?
qa.a: She felt impatient and cross, wanting to go first.

qa.q: Why did Amandeep's question work?
qa.a: It turned waiting into something to be praised, so Rukmini tried hard to stand still.

qa.q: What might Nani feel when Rukmini grins all the way home?
qa.a: Nani is probably relieved and pleased that the waiting ended happily.

grounding: A young child learns to wait her turn in a village shop line, helped by fairness and an adult's praise.

passage: At the ice-cream van in a Madrid park, six children stood in line. Hiroshi was fifth. He bounced on his toes, then tried to slide in beside the girl at the front. 'Hey, the line!' said Javier, who was sixth. Hiroshi's mother touched his shoulder. 'Everyone's waiting, cariño. Count with me.' They counted the children getting cones: one, two, three. 'Good waiting,' she whispered. When Hiroshi finally got his strawberry cone, he turned round and let Javier pick a sprinkle colour first.

qa.q: What place was Hiroshi in the line?
qa.a: Fifth.

qa.q: Why did Hiroshi try to slide in at the front?
qa.a: He felt impatient and excited, finding it hard to wait for the ice cream.

qa.q: How did Hiroshi's mother help him wait?
qa.a: She reminded him everyone was waiting, counted the cones with him and praised his good waiting.

qa.q: How might Javier feel when Hiroshi tried to slide in?
qa.a: Javier probably felt it was unfair, waiting right behind, which is why he spoke up about the line.

grounding: A young child finds waiting in line hard and manages it with a parent's calm help, counting and praise.

passage: The school canteen queue was twenty children long, and Disha had dance rehearsal in ten minutes. She spotted her friend Manoj near the front and slipped in beside him. 'Just holding a place,' she said loudly, to nobody. The boy behind Manoj, a Class 3 kid holding coins, looked at her with big eyes and said nothing. Manoj said, 'Disha, he's been waiting since the bell.' Her face went hot. For a second she wanted to say she was in a hurry and it didn't matter. Then she saw the little boy's coins, counted out carefully. She stepped back and said, 'Sorry, you go.' She reached rehearsal two minutes late, and the teacher let it go.

qa.q: How long was the canteen queue?
qa.a: Twenty children long.

qa.q: What did Disha feel when Manoj spoke up?
qa.a: A flash of guilt and embarrassment, her face hot, with a moment of wanting to defend herself.

qa.q: What helped Disha change course?
qa.a: Manoj naming it plainly, and Disha noticing the little boy's carefully counted coins, which made the unfairness real.

qa.q: What might the Class 3 boy have felt when Disha slipped in?
qa.a: Probably small and upset but too shy to speak, since he had waited since the bell.

grounding: A child in a hurry cuts a queue, feels a flash of guilt when a friend objects, and steps back.

passage: Monday: at the school bus stop, Baljeet ducked in front of three younger kids to grab the window seat. Nobody said anything, and he felt clever. Wednesday: he did it again. This time Saurabh, from the next class, said, 'Back of the line, Baljeet.' Baljeet shrugged. 'Who's going to make me?' He felt defiant, and a little sick. Friday: at the book fair, a bigger boy pushed right in front of Baljeet at the comics table and took the last copy he'd been waiting for. 'Hey! I was here first!' Baljeet shouted. The boy laughed and walked off. On the bus home, Baljeet waited at the back of the line and didn't say why.

qa.q: What did the bigger boy take at the book fair?
qa.a: The last copy of the comic Baljeet had been waiting for.

qa.q: How did Baljeet feel when Saurabh told him to go to the back?
qa.a: Defiant on the outside and a little sick inside, knowing it wasn't fair.

qa.q: What could Baljeet do next time he's in a hurry?
qa.a: Wait his turn, or politely ask the others if he can go ahead, instead of pushing in.

qa.q: How might the three younger kids have felt on Monday?
qa.a: Pushed aside and too small to object, probably annoyed or hurt when Baljeet took the window seat.

grounding: Over a week a child cuts a line with defiance, then feels how it lands when someone cuts in front of him.

passage: Saurabh, you pushed ahead at the cinema counter today, didn't you? Let your Raghav dadu tell you something. When I was ten, in Asansol, we queued every week for kerosene. One morning I was late for a cricket match, so I pushed in front of an old woman with a cane. I thought she wouldn't mind. She didn't say anything. She just looked at me, and the whole line went quiet. The shopkeeper served me, and I ran off with the can, feeling like a thief. At the match I dropped two easy catches. That evening I went back and carried her can home for her. She gave me a sweet and said, 'Next time, just ask.' I've never forgotten her face.

qa.q: What did young Raghav queue for every week?
qa.a: Kerosene.

qa.q: How did young Raghav feel running off with the can?
qa.a: Guilty, like a thief, after the old woman's look and the line going quiet.

qa.q: Which choice in the story shows young Raghav putting things right?
qa.a: Going back that evening to carry the old woman's can home, owning what he had done.

qa.q: What might the old woman have felt when young Raghav pushed in?
qa.a: Probably hurt and tired, but she chose silence and later kindness, telling him, 'Next time, just ask.'

grounding: A grandfather recalls cutting a line as a boy in a hurry and the guilt that followed when others reacted.

passage:
'Two tickets to Charminar, please,' said Hafsa, handing over the coins. 'Thank you, bhaiya.'
The conductor blinked. 'Welcome, madam.'
Avni tugged her sleeve. 'Ammi, why do you always say thank you? It's his job.'
'Because he's been standing since six this morning,' Hafsa said. The bus lurched, and Hafsa's bag bumped a man in the next seat. 'Oh, sorry, uncle.'
'No problem, beti.'
At the stop, a crowd pushed toward the door. Hafsa held Avni's hand and waited. 'Let the grandmother go first.'
'But we'll be last!'
'We'll still get off.'
The next week, on the same bus, Avni handed the conductor her own coins. 'Thank you, bhaiya,' she said, and looked at her mother to see if she'd noticed.

qa.q: Where were Hafsa and Avni going?
qa.a: To Charminar.

qa.q: What does Avni looking at her mother after thanking the conductor suggest?
qa.a: Avni felt proud and hoped Ammi noticed she was copying her good manners.

qa.q: How did Hafsa teach manners without lecturing?
qa.a: By doing it herself: thanking the conductor, apologising for the bump and letting the grandmother go first, with short reasons when asked.

qa.q: How might the conductor feel when thanked?
qa.a: Surprised and a little pleased, since he has been standing since six and rarely hears it.

grounding: A mother teaches public manners by example on a bus, and her daughter copies her the next week.

passage: I used to lecture my daughter Rekha about manners, and it never stuck. Then one Saturday at the vegetable market, I realised she wasn't listening to my words at all; she was watching me. I'd snapped at the vendor about the price of tomatoes, and five minutes later Rekha snapped at her little cousin for taking her ball. Same tone. So I tried something. I started thanking the auto driver, waiting behind the old man at the cash machine without sighing, apologising when my bag bumped someone. I didn't point any of it out. Three weeks later, in the temple queue, Rekha stepped aside for a woman with a baby and said, 'You go first, aunty.' I'm Chetan, and that's the best lesson I never taught.

qa.q: What did Rekha say to the woman with a baby?
qa.a: 'You go first, aunty.'

qa.q: How did Chetan feel after hearing Rekha snap in the same tone?
qa.a: Chetan felt uncomfortable and a bit ashamed, realising Rekha was copying Chetan's behaviour, not the lectures.

qa.q: What changed in Chetan's way of teaching manners?
qa.a: Chetan stopped lecturing and started modelling: thanking the driver, waiting patiently and apologising, without pointing it out.

qa.q: How might the woman with the baby see Rekha?
qa.a: As a kind, thoughtful child, and she was likely grateful to be let ahead in the queue.

grounding: A parent realises children learn manners by watching, and changes their own public behaviour instead of lecturing.

passage: Class 4 trip note, museum visit, Friday. Zainab, a parent volunteer, came with us. At the ticket counter she thanked the guard by the name on his badge. When a school group from elsewhere pushed ahead, she simply waited and said to our children, 'They must be in a hurry; we'll still see everything.' In the café she apologised to a waiter when she knocked a spoon down. I noticed Ojas watching her closely. Later, at the dinosaur gallery, Ojas held the door for an elderly man and said, 'Please go first.' No one had told Ojas to. I will ask Zainab to volunteer again, and on Monday in class we will talk about what the children noticed on the trip.

qa.q: What did Ojas say to the elderly man?
qa.a: 'Please go first.'

qa.q: What might Ojas have been thinking while watching Zainab closely?
qa.a: Ojas seemed curious and impressed by how calmly and kindly Zainab behaved, and quietly decided to copy it.

qa.q: What does the teacher plan, and why is it useful?
qa.a: Asking Zainab to volunteer again and discussing on Monday what the children noticed, so they reflect on the example they saw.

qa.q: How might the guard feel being thanked by name?
qa.a: Surprised and respected, noticed as a person rather than part of the building.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a child copying the calm public manners a parent volunteer modelled on a trip.

passage:
[Group: Bus 14 gang]
Sumit: that uncle on the bus today 😅
Ganga: which one
Sumit: the one who turned round and said 'beta, some of us have headaches'
Ganga: lol we were loud tho
Sumit: we were having FUN
Ganga: ya but Pinky was literally doing the lion roar
Pinky: it was a very good lion roar
Ganga: the aunty with the baby looked so tired 😬
Sumit: ok fine. didn't notice her
Ganga: nobody did. we just forget there's other people on the bus
Sumit: tomorrow indoor voices. except the lion
Pinky: the lion will whisper
Ganga: 🙂

qa.q: What did the uncle say to them on the bus?
qa.a: 'Beta, some of us have headaches.'

qa.q: How did Sumit feel after Ganga mentioned the tired aunty with the baby?
qa.a: Sumit felt a bit sheepish and guilty, admitting nobody had noticed her.

qa.q: What made the uncle's comment work?
qa.a: It was calm and light, not a scolding, so the group could laugh about it and still agree to use indoor voices.

qa.q: What might the bus ride have been like for the aunty with the baby?
qa.a: Tiring and stressful, trying to settle a baby while a group roared and laughed nearby.

grounding: Teenagers enjoying their group's energy are loud on a bus without thinking of others, and a calm word corrects it.

passage: At the touring tent cinema at the Sirsi fair, Bhavna, Leela and four friends sat in the second row, sharing roasted peanuts and commenting on every scene. When the hero fell off his horse, Leela shrieked with laughter, and the others joined in, stamping their feet on the wooden benches. It was the best night of their summer. Behind them, an old farmer leaned forward and said calmly, 'Girls, I've come twenty kilometres for this film. Let me hear the songs, at least.' Bhavna turned red. She hadn't even thought about the people behind. 'Sorry, ajja,' she said. They whispered through the rest, and at the interval Leela offered the farmer some peanuts.

qa.q: How far had the old farmer come for the film?
qa.a: Twenty kilometres.

qa.q: Why did Bhavna turn red?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and a little guilty, realising she hadn't even thought about the people behind them.

qa.q: Why did the farmer's words work so well?
qa.a: He spoke calmly and gave a real reason, so the girls could apologise instead of getting defensive.

qa.q: What might the evening have been like for the farmer before he spoke?
qa.a: Frustrating, having travelled twenty kilometres and being unable to hear the film over the laughter.

grounding: A group of teenage girls, caught up in their fun, is loud at a fair cinema until a calm word from a farmer corrects it.

passage: On the evening train in Mexico City, Diego, Camila and three classmates were replaying the school football final, loudly, with sound effects. Diego acted out his own goal and bumped into a pole. Camila laughed so hard she snorted, which made everyone laugh more. The carriage was packed with people coming home from work. A nurse in blue scrubs, sitting across from them, closed her eyes and rubbed her temples. At the next stop she said quietly, 'Chicos, twelve-hour shift. Could you bring it down a little?' Diego's grin faded. 'Sorry, señora.' They talked in low voices for the rest of the ride. When the nurse got off, Camila said, 'I didn't even see her.'

qa.q: How long was the nurse's shift?
qa.a: Twelve hours.

qa.q: What did Diego feel when the nurse spoke?
qa.a: His grin faded; he felt embarrassed and sorry, realising how loud they had been.

qa.q: What made the nurse's request effective?
qa.a: She asked quietly, gave a reason and didn't scold, so the group lowered their voices willingly.

qa.q: What was the ride like for the nurse before she spoke?
qa.a: Exhausting, with a headache after a long shift and a loud group right across from her.

grounding: Teenagers celebrating loudly on a train forget others around them until a calm request corrects it.

subtype: Queue jumped by a well-connected person [Receiver]
passage: At the university admissions office, Charu and her friend Ira had been in the queue since seven, clutching their files. At eleven, a man in a crisp kurta walked straight past forty students and into the registrar's room, waving a letter. 'Minister's reference,' someone whispered. The clerk stood up and smiled at him. Charu felt heat rise in her chest. Her own file had taken three trips to get right. Ira muttered, 'That's how it works here. Forget it.' Around them, most students looked at the floor. But one older student said loudly, 'Sir, is there a separate line for references?' The clerk ignored him. Charu said nothing. On the way home, though, she wrote to the university's grievance email, and felt a little less small.

qa.q: Since what time had Charu and Ira been in the queue?
qa.a: Since seven.

qa.q: What was Charu feeling when the man walked past?
qa.a: Anger and helplessness, heat rising in her chest after waiting since seven and making three trips.

qa.q: What options did the students have, and which did Charu choose?
qa.a: Accept it like Ira, object aloud like the older student, or complain formally; Charu wrote to the grievance email, a calm and safe way to object.

qa.q: How does Ira seem to see the queue-jumping?
qa.a: As normal and not worth fighting, having learned to accept that 'that's how it works here'.

grounding: A student watches someone with influence skip a long queue, feels angry and helpless, and chooses a way to object.

subtype: Queue jumped by a well-connected person [Receiver]
passage:
Dear Vaibhav,
You asked why I sounded upset on the phone. We were at the government hospital for Maa's scan. We'd been waiting four hours. Then a man walked in with two assistants and a phone to his ear, and the ward attendant took him straight in. Someone said he was a big contractor. Maa squeezed my hand and said, 'Let it go, beta.' I couldn't. I was so angry my hands shook, and so helpless, because what could I do? A lady next to us, waiting with her father, said, 'This happens every time.' That's what scared me: everyone just accepted it.
In the end I asked at reception, calmly, how the order is decided. The nurse looked embarrassed and moved Maa up two places.
I'm still angry.
Shreya

qa.q: How long had Shreya and Maa been waiting?
qa.a: Four hours.

qa.q: What did Shreya feel when the man was taken straight in?
qa.a: So angry her hands shook, and helpless, unsure what she could do.

qa.q: What did Shreya's calm question achieve?
qa.a: Asking reception how the order is decided made the unfairness visible and got Maa moved up two places.

qa.q: How might the lady waiting with her father see the situation?
qa.a: She seems resigned, saying 'This happens every time', having learned to accept the unfairness.

grounding: A young woman waiting at a hospital sees an influential man skip the queue, feels angry and helpless, and chooses to object calmly.

subtype: Queue jumped by a well-connected person [Receiver]
passage: Bhavna, you asked what happened at the exam centre. So, this is Aditi's rant. Three hundred of us in the sun, waiting for the gate to open for document checks. Then a car pulls up, and a boy walks straight to the front with a man everyone called 'the local leader's nephew'. The guard just opened the side gate for him. I felt this hot, useless anger. My father has told me my whole life, 'Don't argue with powerful people.' And for a second I thought, fine, that's the world. But the girl next to me calmly asked the guard, 'Is there a rule for this?' Others joined in. The guard got nervous and sent the boy back to the line. I didn't say anything. I'm still thinking about why.

qa.q: How many students were waiting in the sun?
qa.a: Three hundred.

qa.q: What did Aditi feel when the boy walked to the front?
qa.a: A hot, useless anger mixed with helplessness, and a pull to accept it because of the father's advice.

qa.q: What did the girl next to Aditi do that worked?
qa.a: She calmly asked the guard whether there was a rule, others joined in, and the guard sent the boy back to the line.

qa.q: How might the guard have felt when the students started asking?
qa.a: Nervous and caught between pressure from a powerful family and a crowd asking about fairness.

grounding: A student watches a well-connected boy skip a queue, feels angry and helpless, and sees someone else object calmly.

subtype: Giving up a seat or space [Actor]
passage:
'Finally, seats!' Kalyani dropped onto the bus bench. 'My feet are dead.'
Keerthana sat beside her. 'Same. Ten hours standing at the store.'
At the next stop a woman climbed in, one hand on her belly, the other clutching a steel tiffin.
Keerthana stood up. 'Akka, sit here.'
'No, no, you're tired too,' the woman said.
'You're carrying two people. I'm carrying one.'
The woman laughed and sat. An old man nearby said, 'Good girl, very nice.'
Keerthana shrugged and held the overhead bar.
Kalyani whispered, 'You didn't have to.'
'I know.' Keerthana swayed with the bus. 'My sister had a baby last year. She said nobody ever gave her a seat.'
'Now I feel guilty.'
'Don't. Just next time.'

qa.q: How long had Keerthana been standing at the store?
qa.a: Ten hours.

qa.q: Why did Keerthana give up the seat despite being tired?
qa.a: She felt empathy and concern, remembering her sister saying nobody ever gave her a seat when pregnant.

qa.q: How did Keerthana handle the old man's praise?
qa.a: She shrugged and held the bar, needing no praise for a small act.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling after Keerthana's explanation?
qa.a: Kalyani felt a little guilty for staying seated, and Keerthana gently let it go with 'Just next time'.

grounding: A tired young woman gives her bus seat to a pregnant woman out of awareness and needs no praise for it.

subtype: Giving up a seat or space [Actor]
passage: I used to pretend to be asleep on the metro. Headphones in, eyes shut, so I'd never have to decide whether someone needed my seat. Then one evening an old man with a walking stick stood swaying in front of me for three stations. My colleague Zeenat, standing near the door, was watching. I pretended not to notice. When he nearly fell at a curve, a schoolgirl caught his arm. I felt terrible. The next day I kept my eyes open. When an elderly woman got on with shopping bags, I stood up before thinking about it and said, 'Please, sit.' She smiled and sat. Nobody clapped. Zeenat just nodded at me. I'm Varun, and now I keep my eyes open on the metro.

qa.q: For how many stations did the old man stand in front of Varun?
qa.a: Three stations.

qa.q: How did Varun feel when the schoolgirl caught the old man's arm?
qa.a: Varun felt terrible, guilty and ashamed for pretending not to notice.

qa.q: What small habit did Varun change?
qa.a: Keeping eyes open on the metro, so Varun notices who needs a seat and offers it straight away.

qa.q: What might Zeenat's nod mean?
qa.a: Zeenat seems to have noticed the change and quietly approves, without making a fuss.

grounding: A young adult moves from avoiding notice to giving up a seat for an elderly person, without needing praise.

subtype: Giving up a seat or space [Actor]
passage: Waiting-room note, eye clinic, Monday. Busy morning; every chair taken and fourteen patients standing. Madhav, the young man who brings his grandfather every week, gave up his chair when Minakshi, clearly pregnant and holding a toddler, came in. He did it without a word, just stood and gestured. When the lady beside him said, 'Such a good boy,' he looked embarrassed and moved to the window. His grandfather patted his hand. A few minutes later, two more people stood up for elderly patients. I have asked the office for six more chairs and a priority seating sign by the entrance.

qa.q: How many patients were standing?
qa.a: Fourteen.

qa.q: What does Madhav moving to the window after the praise suggest?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed by the attention; he gave the seat out of awareness, not for praise.

qa.q: What did the note-writer do next, and why?
qa.a: Asked for six more chairs and a priority seating sign, so giving way is easier and doesn't depend on one person.

qa.q: How might Minakshi feel being offered the chair?
qa.a: Relieved and grateful, since she was pregnant and holding a toddler in a full room.

grounding: A clinic note records a young man quietly giving his seat to a pregnant woman, uncomfortable with praise.

passage: The rain was pelting down, the bus was forty minutes late, and the shelter was packed. Dhruv watched a young man in a cricket jersey, whom his friends called Suraj, finish a packet of chips and flick the wrapper into the gutter, where it joined a floating mess. Dhruv's jaw tightened. He thought about saying something, then looked at Suraj's three friends, big and loud. Would it start a fight? The bin was right there, two steps away. Dhruv took a breath and, instead of scolding, said lightly, 'Bin's just behind you, boss. The drain's already crying.' The friends laughed. Suraj rolled his eyes, but he fished the wrapper out with his shoe and dropped it in the bin.

qa.q: How late was the bus?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: What was Dhruv worried about before speaking?
qa.a: Dhruv felt irritated but cautious, worried that speaking up to a group of big, loud friends might start a fight.

qa.q: Why did Dhruv's comment work?
qa.a: It was light and funny, pointing to the bin without scolding, so Suraj could fix it without losing face.

qa.q: How might Suraj have felt when Dhruv spoke?
qa.a: A bit embarrassed in front of his friends, rolling his eyes, but the joke made it easy to pick up the wrapper.

grounding: A commuter sees someone litter, weighs safety and tone, and chooses a light, polite comment that works.

passage: At the Dadar ticket window, the morning line snaked round a pillar. Sudha, on her way to her clinic job, watched a well-dressed woman, Manjula, from the next building, walk up and slide in near the front, pretending to know someone. Behind her, a tired-looking mother with a school bag sighed. Sudha felt the old tug: say something, or not? Manjula knew where she lived. Sudha chose a smile. 'Manjula-tai, the line starts back there, by the pillar. We'll all miss the 8:10 otherwise!' A few people laughed. Manjula flushed, muttered, 'Oh, I didn't see,' and walked to the end. The mother gave Sudha a small nod.

qa.q: Where did the line start?
qa.a: Back by the pillar.

qa.q: What made Sudha hesitate before speaking?
qa.a: Sudha felt uneasy, since Manjula knew where she lived and speaking up might cause trouble between neighbours.

qa.q: What in Sudha's approach made the correction work?
qa.a: A smile, a respectful 'tai' and a light joke about the train, which let Manjula move back without a scene.

qa.q: How might the mother with the school bag feel after Manjula moved?
qa.a: Relieved and grateful, which she showed with a small nod to Sudha.

grounding: A commuter sees a neighbour jump a queue, weighs the risk and uses a light, polite comment that works.

passage:
'Did he just walk past everyone?' Pranav whispered.
Hafsa watched the man in the grey suit slip under the rope at airport security, suitcase rolling. 'Yep.'
'Say something. You're good at that.'
'Maybe he's missing a flight.'
'Or maybe he's rude.'
Hafsa weighed it. The man looked stressed, not dangerous. The staff were busy. She stepped forward and said pleasantly, 'Excuse me, sir, is your flight about to close? The line's back there otherwise.'
The man turned, startled. 'Mine boards in ten minutes.'
A woman in the line said, 'Go ahead, then.'
'Thank you,' the man said, embarrassed. 'Sorry, everyone.'
Pranav stared. 'You didn't even scold him.'
'Didn't need to,' Hafsa said. 'Now we know.'

qa.q: How soon did the man's flight board?
qa.a: In ten minutes.

qa.q: What was Hafsa thinking before stepping forward?
qa.a: Hafsa felt curious and cautious, judging that the man seemed stressed rather than dangerous before choosing to speak.

qa.q: Why was Hafsa's question better than a scolding?
qa.a: It was polite and gave the man a chance to explain, so the line could decide fairly, and he apologised.

qa.q: How might the man in the grey suit have felt when Hafsa spoke?
qa.a: Startled and embarrassed, but relieved to explain and be allowed ahead.

grounding: A traveller sees someone skip a queue, weighs safety and tone, and uses a polite question instead of a scolding.

passage: Nikita, you want to know how to handle line-cutters without a fight? Your Ritu masi has had practice. In 1994 I worked at the post office counter in Jaipur. Every pension day, someone tried to slip in. I learned to smile and say, 'Excuse me, uncle, the line starts at the door. You'll be served soon, promise.' Most people went back, a bit sheepish. One day a man shouted at me, red-faced, that he was an important person. The people in line were getting tense. I didn't argue. I served him quickly, and then apologised to the next woman in line for the wait. Later my boss asked why I'd given in. I said, 'Because a fight in a queue helps nobody.'

qa.q: What did Ritu masi say to line-cutters?
qa.a: 'Excuse me, uncle, the line starts at the door. You'll be served soon, promise.'

qa.q: How might the people in line have felt when the man shouted?
qa.a: Tense and uneasy, worried the shouting would turn into a fight.

qa.q: What choice in the story shows when to let it go?
qa.a: When the man turned hostile, Ritu served him quickly instead of arguing, then apologised to the next woman, keeping everyone safe.

qa.q: How might the woman next in line have felt after Ritu's apology?
qa.a: Probably still annoyed at the man but respected and less upset, since Ritu acknowledged her wait.

grounding: An aunt recalls enforcing a queue with calm, friendly firmness, and letting it go when a man turned hostile.

passage: The line for the free eye camp at the community hall had been growing since dawn, and by noon the heat was brutal. Chetan, a volunteer, was handing out tokens at the door. A young man, Lokesh, walked past thirty elderly people and held out his hand for a token. 'For my grandmother, she's in the auto.' Chetan kept his voice warm. 'Excuse me, bhai, the line starts at the gate. If she can't stand, bring her to the shade and we'll give her a priority token.' Lokesh hesitated, then went to fetch her. She really was frail, and Chetan seated her first. Ten minutes later another man tried the same trick and began shouting when stopped. Chetan let him pass rather than start a fight, and made a note to tell the camp lead.

qa.q: What did Chetan offer Lokesh's grandmother?
qa.a: A priority token, if she was brought to the shade.

qa.q: What might Lokesh have felt when Chetan kindly stopped him?
qa.a: A bit caught out and hesitant, but also relieved to be offered a fair way for his grandmother.

qa.q: How did Chetan balance firmness and safety?
qa.a: He was warm and clear with Lokesh, offering a fair option, but when the second man turned hostile, Chetan let it go and reported it instead of fighting.

qa.q: How might the thirty elderly people in line feel watching this?
qa.a: Reassured that the line mattered, and perhaps uneasy when the shouting man pushed through.

grounding: A volunteer enforces a queue in the heat with calm, friendly firmness, and lets it go when a man turns hostile.

passage: At the busy bakery counter in Lajpat Nagar, the queue was eight deep when Pradeep, phone to his ear, strode to the front and asked for a birthday cake. Alka, next in line, felt a familiar flash of irritation. She kept her voice light. 'Sorry, the queue's that way, just behind the aunty in green.' Pradeep looked round, surprised. 'Oh. Sorry, I didn't see. My daughter's party starts in twenty minutes.' 'Then you'd better hurry,' Alka said, smiling. 'It moves fast.' He laughed and went to the back. The aunty in green said to Alka, 'I'd have shouted.' Alka shrugged. 'Shouting takes longer.' Pradeep got his cake eleven minutes later and waved at her on the way out.

qa.q: How long until Pradeep's daughter's party?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: What did Alka feel when Pradeep strode to the front?
qa.a: A familiar flash of irritation, which she chose to cover with a light voice.

qa.q: What made Alka's approach work?
qa.a: Calm, friendly firmness: pointing to where the queue is, smiling and joking, so Pradeep moved back without a fight.

qa.q: How might the aunty in green see Alka's approach?
qa.a: She would have shouted, so she seems surprised and perhaps impressed that a calm word worked.

grounding: A woman politely enforces a bakery queue with calm, friendly firmness, and it works.

passage: On derby day, Nikita wore her green-and-maroon Kolkata Tigers jersey, two sizes too big, and painted a tiger stripe on each cheek. Their whole lane in Salt Lake had flags on the balconies. When the Tigers scored, the building shook with cheering, and Manjula aunty from downstairs came up banging a steel plate like a drum. Nikita didn't know most of the players' names, but she knew the song. She sang it with the aunties, the uncles and the boys from the corner shop, all of them jumping at once. 'We're Tigers!' she shouted, and for that moment she was, along with everyone else.

qa.q: What did Nikita paint on her cheeks?
qa.a: A tiger stripe on each cheek.

qa.q: How did Nikita feel singing the song with everyone?
qa.a: Joyful and proud, as if she truly belonged to the Tigers crowd, even without knowing the players' names.

qa.q: How could Nikita's family keep derby day friendly?
qa.a: Cheer loudly for the Tigers while staying kind to neighbours who support the other team.

qa.q: What might the derby mean for Manjula aunty?
qa.a: A chance to celebrate with the whole building, banging a plate and sharing the children's excitement.

grounding: A child wears her team's colours and sings with the neighbourhood, feeling instant belonging.

passage:
'Veer Pratap is the best hero ever,' Sumit announced, pulling on his cap with the golden lightning bolt.
'Your hero can't even dance,' said Imran.
'He saved a whole train in Part Two!'
'With a rope. Anyone can do that.'
The other boys on the school steps laughed. Sumit's ears went red. 'You're just jealous because your hero's films are boring.'
Anil held up his own lightning-bolt pencil box. 'I like Veer Pratap too.'
'See?' Sumit grinned. 'Veer Pratap Club. Me and Anil.'
'And me,' said little Gaurav, who hadn't seen any of the films.
Imran rolled his eyes, then smiled. 'Fine. But when the next one comes out, we're all watching it together, and I'm going to laugh at the train scene.'
'Deal,' said Sumit.

qa.q: What was on Sumit's cap?
qa.a: A golden lightning bolt.

qa.q: Why did Sumit's ears go red?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and defensive when the boys laughed at his hero.

qa.q: How did the boys turn the argument into something friendly?
qa.a: By agreeing to watch the next film together, so different favourites could still be shared.

qa.q: Why might little Gaurav join the Veer Pratap Club without seeing any films?
qa.a: He wanted to belong to the group, and loving the same hero is an easy way in.

grounding: Children cheer for a film hero and form an instant club, since loving the same thing gives belonging.

passage: When I was ten, my whole world was the Punjab Panthers kabaddi team. I had the yellow headband, the poster over my bed and every raider's name memorised. On match nights, my friend Pranav and I sat on his roof with a small radio and screamed at every tackle. At school, anyone who wore a Panthers badge was instantly my friend, even kids from other classes I'd never spoken to. Once the Panthers lost the final, and I cried under my blanket. Pranav came over the next morning with two cups of tea and said, 'Next season.' It wasn't really about kabaddi. It was about being part of something loud and yellow and ours. I'm Baljeet, and I still have the headband.

qa.q: What did Baljeet and Pranav listen to the matches on?
qa.a: A small radio, on Pranav's roof.

qa.q: How did Baljeet feel when the Panthers lost the final?
qa.a: Heartbroken, sad enough to cry under the blanket.

qa.q: How could Baljeet keep the fun of fandom healthy?
qa.a: Enjoy the team and the friendships it brings, while remembering that losses pass and friends like Pranav matter most.

qa.q: What might Pranav's 'Next season' mean to Baljeet?
qa.a: Comfort and loyalty; Pranav shared the love and the loss, and came to say they were still in it together.

grounding: A child's love for a team gives instant belonging and a shared story with friends.

passage: Vandana's school bag was covered in Neon Monsoon pins, and her phone wallpaper was the band's latest album cover. In her Pune classroom she was 'the Monsoon girl', and she liked it. Online she had friends in five cities who knew every lyric. So when Rashmi said at lunch, 'Their new song is honestly just noise,' Vandana's face went hot. 'You don't even understand their music,' she snapped, louder than she meant. The table went quiet. Rashmi raised her hands. 'Okay! It's just a song.' It wasn't just a song to Vandana. She spent the afternoon replaying the words, as if Rashmi had insulted her and not a band. That night she messaged Rashmi: 'Sorry I snapped. They just mean a lot to me.'

qa.q: What was on Vandana's phone wallpaper?
qa.a: The band's latest album cover.

qa.q: Why did Vandana snap at Rashmi?
qa.a: She felt hurt and defensive, as if criticism of the band was an attack on her.

qa.q: What did Vandana do that helped the friendship afterwards?
qa.a: She messaged Rashmi to apologise for snapping and explained that the band means a lot to her.

qa.q: How might Rashmi have felt when Vandana snapped?
qa.a: Surprised and a little hurt, since she thought she was just sharing an opinion about a song.

grounding: A teenager's favourite band becomes part of who she is, so criticism of it feels personal.

passage:
'Dinner, Ishita!' Rashmi called.
'Two minutes, Mumma, the finale thread is live!'
'What finale?'
'The Glass Crown. The series. The one I've watched four times.' Ishita came to the table in a T-shirt printed with a cracked crown. 'Everyone in the fandom is losing it.'
Her brother Kartik smirked. 'It's a show about sad people in capes.'
Ishita put her fork down. 'Don't. You don't get it.'
'It's just a show—'
'It's not just a show! Those people online are the only ones who understand me!'
The table went quiet. Rashmi reached across and touched her hand. 'Then tell me what it's about. Properly. I want to understand too.'
Ishita blinked, then slowly began explaining the first episode.

qa.q: How many times had Ishita watched the series?
qa.a: Four times.

qa.q: What does Ishita's outburst about 'the only ones who understand me' suggest?
qa.a: She feels deeply attached and defensive, as if mocking the show mocks her, and somewhat lonely outside the fandom.

qa.q: What did Rashmi do that calmed things?
qa.a: She touched Ishita's hand and asked her to explain the show properly, showing interest instead of dismissing it.

qa.q: How might Kartik see Ishita's reaction?
qa.a: He probably meant it as teasing and was surprised by how personally she took it.

grounding: A teenager's favourite series has become part of her identity, and teasing about it feels personal.

passage: At fifteen, I was the biggest fan of the Riverfall books in our school. I'd read all seven twice, written fan fiction, and joined an online group of three thousand readers. I signed my notebooks with the heroine's name. So when Naveen said in English class that the books were 'badly written and overrated', I felt as if he'd slapped me. I argued so hard that the teacher had to stop me. Later I realised I'd said more that day than in the whole term. Naveen wasn't insulting me. He was talking about books. But the books were so tied up with who I was that I couldn't tell the difference. I'm Shreya. I still love Riverfall. I just try to remember I'm more than a fan.

qa.q: How many readers were in the online group?
qa.a: Three thousand.

qa.q: How did Shreya feel when Naveen called the books overrated?
qa.a: Shreya felt as if slapped, hurt and defensive, as though the criticism was personal.

qa.q: What could Shreya do the next time someone criticises a favourite thing?
qa.a: Pause and remember they're talking about the thing, not about Shreya, then share a view calmly.

qa.q: How might Naveen have seen Shreya's reaction in class?
qa.a: He was only giving an opinion about books, so he was likely surprised by how hard Shreya argued.

grounding: A teenager's favourite book series becomes part of who they are, so criticism of it feels like a personal attack.
